client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't seem to enjoy it the way I used to, because all I can think about is that she's not there. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, honestly, because nothing is going to bring her back.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — the grief you're carrying sounds really heavy, and it makes complete sense that her absence feels so present at family gatherings where she used to be part of the picture. You're absolutely right that nothing will bring her back, and I want you to know I'm not here to try to "fix" that or take the pain away. I'm wondering, though — when you're at those gatherings and the thought of her absence comes up, what does that thought feel like in your body, and what do you find yourself doing with it?

client: It's like this tight, hollow feeling in my chest, almost like something's been scooped out. And what do I do with it? Honestly, I just kind of go quiet and pull away from everyone else at the gathering, like I'm physically there but I've checked out completely. I end up feeling guilty about that too, because I know my family is grieving her as well and I should probably be connecting with them instead of retreating into myself.
therapist: That hollow, scooped-out feeling you're describing is such a vivid and honest way to capture grief, and the way you withdraw makes complete sense as a way of protecting yourself when the pain feels overwhelming. I want to gently notice something, though — you're carrying not just the grief itself, but also a layer of guilt on top of it for how you're coping, which sounds exhausting. I'm curious, when you imagine what your grandmother would say if she could see you at one of those gatherings, struggling the way you are — what do you think she'd want for you?

client: I've been sitting with that question for a second, and honestly... I think she'd want me to be okay, to laugh and be with the family like we used to. But that almost makes it worse, you know? Because I'm not doing that, I'm failing at the one thing she'd want for me, and now I feel even more guilty on top of everything else.
therapist: It's so tender that you know her well enough to answer that question, and that love for her clearly runs very deep. I want to gently challenge that word "failing" though — you're one month out from losing someone you deeply loved, and grief isn't a performance you can succeed or fail at; it's something that moves through you at its own pace. What do you think it would feel like to offer yourself even a small fraction of the compassion your grandmother would so clearly want to give you right now?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it also feels kind of... hollow, I guess? Like, telling myself to have compassion for my grief doesn't actually make the loneliness go away at night when I reach for my phone to call her and then remember I can't. I think what scares me is that if I stop being hard on myself about it, I'll just fall apart completely and there won't be anyone there to catch me.
therapist: That moment of reaching for your phone to call her and then remembering — that's one of the most painful kinds of grief, and it makes complete sense that self-compassion feels abstract and hollow compared to something that real and immediate. And that fear of falling apart if you let your guard down is so understandable, but I'm gently wondering if the self-criticism is actually holding you together, or if it might be adding weight to something that's already very heavy to carry. What do you imagine "falling apart" would actually look like — and is there a part of you that's maybe already surviving something you didn't think you could?

client: I think "falling apart" looks like not being able to get out of bed, not showing up to work, just... completely losing the thread of my life. And yeah, maybe I am surviving something I didn't think I could, but it doesn't feel like surviving, it feels more like just going through motions without her in it. The self-criticism thing you said — I hear you, but honestly it's the only thing that feels like it's keeping me functional, like if I stop being hard on myself for not calling her more when she was alive, I'm somehow letting myself off the hook for something I can't undo.
therapist: That guilt about not calling more — that's such a heavy thing to carry, and I want to reflect something back to you: the fact that you wish you'd called more is itself evidence of how much you loved her, and love and regret so often travel together precisely because we care deeply. I'm also noticing that you've gotten out of bed, you've shown up to work, and you're here right now talking about something really painful — that's not just "going through motions," even if it feels that way. I'm wondering, if a close friend came to you carrying the same guilt about their grandmother, would you tell them they needed to keep punishing themselves to prove their love, or would you see it differently for them than you do for yourself?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, if a friend came to me with that guilt, I'd probably tell them they were being too hard on themselves. But it feels different when it's me — like I don't deserve that same kind of understanding, because I'm the one who actually didn't make those calls. I know that probably sounds like I'm just rejecting what you're offering, but the logic in my head keeps saying that my friend's situation would somehow be more forgivable than mine.
therapist: You're not rejecting what I'm offering at all — you're actually doing something really important right now, which is noticing that there are two different sets of rules in your head: one generous and forgiving for people you love, and one much harsher for yourself. That gap is worth paying attention to, because it tells us something — not that you're unforgivable, but that somewhere along the way you learned that you have to earn the same compassion you'd freely give to others. I'm curious, where do you think that belief that you're somehow less deserving of understanding came from — does it feel familiar from other parts of your life, or does it feel like something grief has brought up specifically?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, because honestly... yeah, it does feel familiar. I think even as a kid I got the message that I needed to justify my place, like I had to be useful or good enough to deserve care from people. Grief didn't create that, I think it just ripped off whatever was covering it up.
therapist: What you just said takes real courage and insight — recognizing that grief didn't create this wound but simply uncovered something much older is a profound and important realization. That little kid who learned they had to earn care deserved so much better, and I want you to know that the standard you were held to back then wasn't fair or true, even if it's felt like the rules of the world ever since. I'm wondering, as you sit with that recognition right now, what does it feel like to see that younger version of yourself through the same compassionate eyes you'd offer a friend?

client: It's... strange, because part of me wants to feel that compassion, but another part of me immediately pushes back and says that kid should have tried harder, should have been easier to love. Like even now I'm defending the people who made me feel that way, which I know sounds messed up. It's easier to be kind to a friend than to that version of me, because I still feel like I'm somehow responsible for what happened.
therapist: What you're describing doesn't sound messed up at all — when we're young and the people we depend on make us feel we have to earn love, our minds often protect us by deciding *we* were the problem, because it's less frightening than accepting that the people who were supposed to care for us fell short. That belief kept you safe then, but it sounds like it's become a very heavy thing to carry into adulthood, layered now with grief on top of it. I'm gently wondering — what would it mean for you, or what might you have to let go of, if you allowed yourself to consider that maybe that child wasn't responsible at all?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Because if I let myself believe the kid wasn't responsible... then I have to accept that my mom just, what, didn't love me the way I needed? And I don't know if I can sit with that, because at least when it was my fault, there was something I could have done differently, some version of me that could have fixed it.
therapist: What you just named is one of the most painful paradoxes of childhood wounds — that self-blame, as cruel as it is, actually offers a kind of hope, because if it was your fault then there was a version of the story where you could have been enough. Letting go of that blame means grieving not just your grandmother, but also the mother you needed and perhaps didn't fully have, and that's a profound loss that deserves just as much tenderness. I'm here with you in this, and I'm wondering — does it feel like there's any space, even a small one, to hold both things at once: that you couldn't have fixed it, and that your need for that love was completely valid?

client: I think what you're saying makes sense, and part of me wants to hold onto that... but it's hard because if I let go of the blame, it almost feels like I'm saying it didn't matter, like I'm just giving up on ever being understood by her. And then there's this other part that's scared — if it really wasn't my fault, then I have to accept that she just... didn't show up, and I don't know if I'm ready to sit with that.
therapist: Letting go of blame isn't the same as saying it didn't matter — in fact, it might be the most honest way of saying it mattered enormously, that you deserved so much more than you received. And that fear of accepting she didn't show up the way you needed — that's not giving up, that's actually one of the bravest and most painful things a person can face, and you don't have to rush toward it or be ready all at once. I'm wondering, what would it feel like to just sit with the "not yet" — to acknowledge that this truth might be real without having to fully accept it today?
